# A short history of the HP 2000 and HP 2100

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

This is background for the emulators in this project. It is a summary in our own words
of what is publicly known, mostly from Wikipedia's articles (see Sources at the end)
and from the HP manuals (scanned at <https://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/hp/2000TSB/>). Wikipedia can be wrong, so the facts that
matter to the emulator (instruction set, device behaviour) were checked against the
SIMH simulator and the manuals, not against this page.

## Where the hardware came from

- In the early 1960s a group inside Hewlett-Packard wanted a computer to control its
  test systems. Talks with DEC went nowhere, and in 1964 HP bought a five-person Detroit company, Data Systems Inc (DSI), owned by Union Carbide.
  The design became HP's first computer. The work was done in the Dymec division and
  then in a Cupertino division of its own.
- It was sold as a minicomputer by calling it an "instrument controller", because the
  company's founders were not keen on the word minicomputer.
- The **2116A** (shown in November 1966) was a 16-bit machine built with integrated
  circuits and magnetic core memory, with room for 16 plug-in cards (more with an
  external cage). It sold much faster to business and data processing customers than to
  the instrumentation market it was meant for, so cheaper cut-down versions (2115A in
  1967, 2114A in 1968) followed, and then the **2100A** in 1971 with a microcoded CPU,
  hardware multiply and divide, memory protect and a two-channel DMA controller. The
  **2100S** (1973) was a 2100A bundled with floating point, a time base generator and a
  teleprinter interface. Those are the machines this project emulates.
- In 1974 the **21MX** series replaced core with semiconductor memory (and later added
  memory mapping up to a million words), and at the end of 1976 the whole family was
  renamed the **HP 1000**, aimed at real-time work, and carried on until the early 1990s.
  The 2100 line was declared obsolete in 1978. Some tens of thousands were sold, which
  made HP the fourth largest minicomputer maker of the 1970s.

## The HP 2000 time-sharing systems

- The HP 2000 was a 2100-family computer packaged with a terminal multiplexer, disc and
  tape so that many people could use BASIC at once, each at a teletype. **The 2000A** was
  announced in 1968 and described in the Hewlett-Packard Journal that July. It is
  generally described as the first minicomputer to offer time-shared BASIC.
- Versions through the 1970s were named by letter: 2000A, 2000B, 2000C, High-Speed 2000C,
  2000E, 2000F, and the later "2000/Access" (also called Access BASIC in some
  publications; the manual number 22687). The 2000A and 2000E used one processor
  (Wikipedia's two articles disagree about the 2000A; one says it used a separate 2114
  as a terminal server). The others use **two computers**: a larger one runs the BASIC system and owns the discs,
  and a smaller one, the I/O processor, runs the serial lines of the users. Depending on
  the configuration there were up to 16 or up to 32 users. This is why the 2000F and
  Access emulators here run two CPUs.
- A 2000F cost about $105,000 in 1974. Sales of the series stopped in June 1978, and HP
  supported it until about 1985.
- User names are a letter and three digits (B001), and account `A000` is the
  superuser, which is why the library in this project lives in account A000.
  The usual terminal was a Teletype model 33, and programs could be saved and loaded on
  its paper tape. Lines are printed 72 columns wide.

## What HP Time-Shared BASIC was like

HP Time-Shared BASIC (TSB) is a BASIC in the Dartmouth tradition, with differences that
matter when you try to run programs from other systems:

- **Strings are arrays of characters** with a fixed size from `DIM`, and substrings are cut
  with `A$[2,5]` (or round brackets), not with `LEFT$`/`MID$`/`RIGHT$`. Assigning to a
  substring is allowed. `CONVERT` moves between strings and character codes, and a
  quote mark in front of a number (`'65`) gives that character code in a string.
- **Computed jumps** are `GOTO N OF 10,20,30`, not `ON N GOTO`.
- **`#`** is accepted for "not equal", relational operators return 0 or 1 inside
  expressions, and a line holds one statement only (no colons).
- Adjacent string constants in a `PRINT` need no separator in many versions (the Access
  system of this project refuses `"A""B"`, which is one of the library repairs).
- **`MAT` statements** work on whole arrays, `ENTER` is an `INPUT` with a time limit, and
  `LIN(n)` and `TAB(n)` position the output.
- Programs are saved in tokenised form with `SAVE` (or compiled with `CSAVE`), names are
  up to six letters and digits, and everything is stored by account.

Many other BASICs borrowed the HP way of handling strings, among them Apple's Integer
BASIC, Atari BASIC and North Star BASIC, while Altair BASIC and so Microsoft BASIC
followed DEC's. That is why converting programs between the two families is awkward.

## The contributed library and Star Trek

HP kept a catalogue of programs written by customers, called the **Contributed Program
Library**, and customers could order them on paper tape for a small charge. It was one
of the first software libraries of its kind and is the source of the 1054 programs in
this project. The 1974 index and the library documentation volumes are in
<https://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/hp/2000TSB/>.

The best known item is **Star Trek**. Mike Mayfield wrote the first version in 1971 as a
high school student on a different mainframe, and rewrote it in HP BASIC on an HP 2000C
in a local HP sales office; it was finished on 20 October 1972 and entered in the library
in February 1973 as **STTR1**, which is in this library too. David Ahl then ported it to
DEC BASIC and published it in the book *101 BASIC Computer Games*, and from there it
reached almost every early personal computer. The People's Computer Company also
published programs in HP 2000 format, in its newsletter and in the book *What to Do
After You Hit Return* (1975), which is part of the reason HP's dialect became a common
way to write BASIC listings.

## Timeline

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1964 | HP buys Data Systems Inc and starts its computer group |
| 1966 | HP 2116A shown (November) |
| 1967 to 1968 | Cheaper 2115A and 2114A |
| 1968 | HP 2000A time-shared BASIC system announced |
| 1971 | HP 2100A; Mike Mayfield starts Star Trek on another machine |
| 1972 | Star Trek finished in HP BASIC on a 2000C (20 October) |
| 1973 | 2100S; Star Trek enters the HP contributed library as STTR1 (February) |
| 1974 | 21MX series with semiconductor memory; the 2000F costs about $105,000 |
| 1976 | The family is renamed the HP 1000 |
| 1978 | HP 2000 stops selling (June); the 2100 is declared obsolete |
| 1985 | End of HP support for the 2000 systems |
| 1990s | The last HP 1000 models |

## How this relates to the emulators

- **2000E** (one processor, a 7900 disc and paper tapes) was the first system built here
  and is archived. **2000F** (rev 1410/1710) and **2000/Access** (rev 1812) are the live
  systems; both are two-computer systems and run the real HP system software from the
  SIMH kits.
- The emulated machines are 2100-series computers (the 2100S as the main computer for the
  2000F, as in HP's own configuration). On a PicoCalc they run at roughly 0.5 million
  instructions a second, slower than the original hardware; see `README.md` and
  `docs/LESSONS-LEARNED.md`.
